description: Walking through one of the remaining Black Ash forests in this area I appreciate them for being here for what they are. Black Ash is actually one of my favorite trees and I love it for it's historical importance and cultural uses by Natives+pioneers. I've always found the general form to be much more attractive then our other native Ashes. Still when I walk through this area, and other areas dominated by Ash in the understory, I understand these areas are very much human created landscapes. While these mature Ash are quite beautiful in their form, taking a step back, one realizes how unhealthy this ecosystem really is. The most obvious is the ground layer. The soils are practically all bare, and the root flares on the trees are all exposed. In the overstory, the line "For the maples want more sunlight and the oaks ignore their pleas" no longer hold true. The complex processes/relationships between plant and animal kingdoms is all but gone. To quote someone smarter than myself- "The land is dead."-- I can't help but wonder how the functional extinction of Ash will effect the broader landscape. While I don't wish to propose that the disappearance of any species is a good thing, I do wonder how it could have the potential for restoration. In areas where Ash are largely overabundant (almost everywhere), does this give the opportunity for the landscape to heal itself? Realistically, in most areas, this will only allow for more pioneers to move in (Boxelder, Cottonwood, Buckthorn, etc.) but possibly a few Cherry, Willow, and Oak(???) here and there? Perhaps seeing a vast expanse of dead trees will finally give the general public their awakening that something is wrong with the way we manage our land.

description: White Ash - Fraxinus americana (female tree of this dioecious species) I did a series to document the ID of this species, which can be a little confounding, at least to me. This tree was found with samaras in a suburban woodlot in Durham NC (USA). Soil is hydric to mesic at that location. The other species to be expected in this area is Green Ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica). Characters I see indicating Fraxinus americana vs. pennsylvanica are: - leaves whitish (glaucous) beneath, "minutely honeycombed-reticulate" at high magnification (Weakley); with "dense minute rounded projections" (Duncan and Duncan) - bud sits within the U-shaped scar, i.e., upper edge of leaf scars deeply notched, or "petiole bases and leaf scars V- to U- or crescent-shaped with a deeply concave or notched upper margin" (Weakley and most references, but a variable character!) - terminal buds obtuse, with 4-6 brownish scales (Duncan and Duncan) - "samaras 25-32 mm long, samara wings 3-5 mm wide, samara bodies (5-) 6-11 mm long, 1.5-2.5 mm wide; twigs, petioles, petiolules, and rachises glabrous" (Weakley) References - Carolina Nature (Will Cook) www.carolinanature.com/trees/fram.html - Duncan and Duncan, Trees of the Southeastern United States (Univ. Georgia Press, 1988), p. 57-59, plates 45, 47 - Weakley, Flora of the Southeastern United States (UNC Herbarium, 2020), p. 1291

description: Emerald Ash Borers have now killed most of the ash trees in my area. However, I have a two-trunked specimen in my woods -- each trunk about 12" DBH -- that is healthy enough to be dropping fruit. It lost one trunk to the borers, and the second trunk lost most of its crown, but it's hanging in there. Green Ash (F. pennsylvanica) and white ash (F. americana) are the most common species in my area. These white ash fruit are distinctive because the fat seed sticks out on its own at the base of the wing. In most other ash species, the seed is longer and narrower and the wing extends along half or more of its length. Ash fruit may not look that exciting to humans, but things like cardinals and chipmunks enjoy the large seeds.

description:
Hand counted about 120 individuals (primarily seedlings, with a few saplings, and 3-4 mature trees) west of ATV trail before I switched to estimating population based on the size of the area and high frequency of seedlings. 
Within the area, I would estimate
300+ seedlings 
25-40 mature trees with dbh ranging from 4"-12" with a few individuals over 12".

At least 8 trees with seeds still visible in the canopy, meaning the population appears to be reproducing. I would estimate of the larger trees (6"+ dbh) most (70-80%) looked alive. This is in contrast to the other ash species I've observed this year in southern Wisconsin, where most individuals are dead/dying. The other species of ash trees at this site had visibly dead and decaying canopies with few branches left. So anecdotally, my observations match the research that shows Fraxinus quadrangulata has some resistance to EAB.


I stayed on public land and did not survey the abutting private land, so it's possible the population extends farther north. I did briefly survey south and to the northwest continuing on public land, but did not find any separate populations in those directions.

*Mature trees were identified using telephoto lens and observing square/winged stems in canopy.

description:
I was surprised to see nearly all of the canopy blue ash trees were leafing out, compared to zero canopy leaf out for the white and green ash (they had suckers leafing out). Some black ash at the site of <6" diameter were leafing out, but larger trees were not. 

Regeneration of blue ash seemed abundant in the center of the population, with 5+ seedlings in some quadrats there. Most quadrats in the dense center of the population were 0-1 per quadrat. This dense area had all sizes from seedling to mature canopy trees and was about 150m x 120m or about 4-5 acres total. Overall the population covered around 40 acres, with much of that having occasional seedlings or smaller trees, typically 0 per quadrat for the less dense area of the population.  I estimated around 0.25 individuals per quadrat over the densest area, with some wiggle room in that number to cover the sparser areas. 

Since this site seems to be studied closely, many of the target population were marked with paint and individually tagged with ID numbers. Based on this numbering system, I would guess there are at least 100 individuals over about 6" diameter. I would guess many of those are still producing seeds, but because of the timing of my visit, last years seeds had fallen and the trees were not yet in flower, so I can't say for certain how many are producing seeds. I could see last year's seed stalks/peduncles in some of the trees I checked, so the "number in fruit" reflects the trees I  individually verified.
I noticed a few of the trees marked with paint, and even one of the tagged trees were not blue ash but a different species of ash, and also blue ash are only marked within a portion of the population, so the markings cannot be relied on solely.

I observed only a couple mature (>6" diameter) blue ash trees that were dead and standing or had fallen. One was the large (>12" diameter) tree pictured in the photos. Its buds from last season were visible, and it didn't have a dead, rotted crown like other species of ash, so don't know what the cause was.

What's unclear to me is if the blue ash I saw leafing out will all leaf out completely, or if they have partial dieback of the crowns. On a few trees, I could see sections of the tree had new leaves appearing in the canopy, but some sections did not yet.

description: In a large, mature, mostly publicly owned forest tract on a gradual north-facing slope, dominated by red oak and red maple, uncommon for Worcester County. Mature, tall white pine occurs  in small patches mostly on the east side, where 200 year old stone walls are prominent, some of which are double wide indicating formerly plowed fields and the presence of deeper, richer soil. An additional feature is the complete absence of woody invasive species. Mountain laurel and witch hazel are uncommon, in contrast to much of the surrounding area forests. White birch is more common than black birch, another unusual feature. White ash is occasional, some have been attacked by emerald ash borer and are dying out. Hemlock is occasional and no longer casting a deep shade, having been affected by hemlock wooly adelgid. Since I had a metric diameter tape handy, I decided to use it, both to give a more accurate sense of this stand, and to allow future biologists to directly compare. Tape shows diameter in centimeters and millimeters, to which I will add inches in the notes. See all my 19 observations on this date to get a full sense of the stand.
